Volume 07 · Chapter 12

Forensic analysis and accounting integration

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v07-c11

By the endDiagnose a business using reconciled accounts and explicit alternative explanations.

Capability and prerequisites

After this chapter, you can diagnose a business using reconciled accounts, distinguish an accounting correction from a cash event, test a precisely defined covenant, and state competing explanations with the evidence needed to distinguish them. Read accounting standards, disclosure and comparability. Use the earlier chapters' double entry, operating-cycle, tax, relevant-cost, ratio and forecasting tools. A diagnosis should survive tracing an adjustment through every affected statement.

Suppose a profitable supplier reports rising receivables, modest operating cash and comfortable debt headroom. Management attributes the cash gap to growth and presents a larger adjusted profit. Those observations can coexist with a viable business, an innocent cut-off error, weak collection, or intentional misstatement. A spreadsheet can reconcile the figures and expose the consequences of a correction. It cannot establish intent from a ratio.

1. Begin with assertions and alternatives

Forensic analysis here means a disciplined examination of records, economic explanations and contradictory evidence. It does not mean that the learner is performing a statutory audit, authenticating every document, or making a legal determination. A red flag is an observation that warrants investigation. A misstatement is a departure from the applicable recognition, measurement, presentation or disclosure requirement. Whether a misstatement was intentional is a different question.

The U.S. PCAOB's AS 2401, paragraphs .05 and .11–.13, distinguishes intentional fraud from error and explains why suspicious conditions can have other causes. Its audit context also makes clear that even an audit does not supply absolute assurance. We use those boundaries to discipline our reasoning; this chapter supplies neither an audit opinion nor a fraud verdict.

Define the entity, reporting period, currency, consolidation boundary and question before calculating. Reconcile opening balances, transactions and closing balances. Separate three tasks: correct a demonstrable accounting error under stated rules; construct a transparent economic scenario; and assess what evidence remains missing. Do not use a favorable normalization to avoid correcting an error. Do not assume that an internally consistent statement describes real transactions.

One observation can support several hypotheses
ObservationPotential benign explanationPotential adverse explanationDiscriminating evidence
Receivables rise faster than annual salesLate-year genuine sales or agreed longer termsCollection deterioration, premature or fictitious salesMonthly sales cohorts, acceptance terms, aging and subsequent settlement of specific invoices
Inventory grows while cash is weakStock for signed seasonal orders or longer lead timesObsolescence, excess production or incorrect countsPhysical quantities, aging, order conversion, selling prices and write-down assumptions
Operating cash improves sharplyCollection improvement or efficient inventory useDelayed supplier payments, factoring, classification changes or reduced necessary maintenancePayment calendar, supplier terms, financing arrangements and a consistent cash-flow bridge
Adjusted earnings repeatedly exclude costsA genuinely unusual event with a documented boundaryRoutine economic costs excluded asymmetricallyMulti-year adjustments, gains as well as losses, contracts and the activities required to earn revenue

These are alternative hypotheses, not estimated probabilities. Revenue and receivables alone do not identify collection quality. Strong subsequent cash collection supports recoverability of the matched balance, but does not by itself establish that the service was performed before year-end. Different assertions require different evidence.

2. Close the accounts before explaining the cash gap

Case contract. Atlas Field Systems is an original fictional single entity. All monetary amounts are kCU, thousands of fictional currency units. The period is one year. There are no acquisitions, foreign-exchange effects, leases, disposals, deferred taxes, noncash financing, other comprehensive income or unlisted accounts. Inventory and trade payables relate only to the supplied cost of sales. Other operating expenses apart from depreciation settle in cash; inventory purchases follow the specified trade-payables roll-forward, and sales may remain receivable. Tax payments follow the separate rule below. Interest is paid and classified in operating cash under the case's chosen presentation. Capital spending is investing cash; debt principal, dividends and new equity are financing cash.

The fictional tax rule is current tax at 20% of the corrected book pretax profit, with no permanent or temporary differences. Tax paid during the year is a separately observed 16. No refund or tax-loss case is modeled. Corrections change the current tax expense and payable, not that historical payment. These are supplied teaching conventions, not the tax law or reporting requirements of any jurisdiction.

In this restricted setting, with Δ meaning closing minus opening:

CFO = net income + depreciation − Δreceivables − Δinventory + Δtrade payables + Δcurrent tax payable.
Customer receipts = revenue − Δreceivables.
Supplier payments = cost of sales + Δinventory − Δtrade payables.

The identities follow from each account's roll-forward. For example, opening receivables + revenue − customer receipts = closing receivables. Purchases first enter inventory and payables; payment reduces payables and cash. Replacing current tax expense with cash paid requires adding the tax-payable movement. The IFRS Foundation's public IAS 7 overview explains the distinction between direct cash receipts/payments and an indirect adjustment of profit. Our compact formula is not universal: acquisitions, FX, write-offs, gains, deferred taxes and reclassifications require their own adjustments. Taking two unadjusted balance sheets and mechanically calling every difference cash would be wrong.

Worked example 1: profitable, cash constrained, and fully reconciled

Atlas's opening balance sheet and uncorrected year-end draft, kCU
AccountOpeningDraft closing
Cash8054
Trade receivables120200
Inventory100150
Net property, plant and equipment300320
Total assets600724
Trade payables90120
Current tax payable012
Debt principal250230
Equity260362
Liabilities plus equity600724

The draft income statement shows revenue 1,000, cost of sales 600, net cash operating expense 200, depreciation 40, interest 20 and current tax 28. Net cash operating expense is cash payments of 215 less a separate supplier-settlement cash recovery of 15. The payments include ordinary operations 170, recurring marketing 25 and severance 20. Thus EBITDA—here simply earnings before interest, tax and depreciation—is 200, EBIT is 160, pretax profit is 140 and net income is 112. There is no amortization in this case.

The indirect bridge is 112 + 40 − 80 − 50 + 30 + 12 = CFO 64. The operating-cycle balances absorb 80 + 50 − 30 = 100; depreciation and the tax-payment lag offset 52 of that absorption relative to profit. Calling the entire 48 profit-minus-CFO gap “uncollected sales” would ignore inventory, supplier credit and tax timing.

Independently, customer receipts are 1,000 − 80 = 920. Inventory purchases are 600 + 50 = 650; supplier payments are 650 − 30 = 620. Cash operations are 920 − 620 − 215 + 15 − 20 − 16 = 64. The direct and indirect statements describe the same cash events.

Capital spending is 60, debt principal paid is 20, and dividends are 10. Consequently cash closes at 80 + 64 − 60 − 20 − 10 = 54. PPE closes at 300 + 60 − 40 = 320. Equity closes at 260 + 112 − 10 = 362. Tax payable is 28 − 16 = 12. Every opening stock, flow and closing stock agrees.

The defined measure CFO less capital spending is only 4. Principal and dividends then reduce cash by a further 30. EBITDA of 200 is not cash available for distribution. The business may have expanded profitably while funding receivables and stock, but that hypothesis requires sales, collection and inventory evidence. Arithmetic closure establishes consistency, not that every revenue entry is earned.

3. Correct an error through all statements, then retest the contract

Distinguish a new estimate from an error established by available evidence, and verify the applicable reporting rules as taught in Chapter 11. Here the statements are an unissued draft. The case gives explicit recognition facts so the learner can calculate the correction without speculating about an accounting framework. A real revision of issued accounts requires the appropriate dated standards and process.

Worked example 2: a cut-off correction changes headroom without changing cash

A 40 entry in draft revenue and receivables relates to installation service scheduled and accepted in January. At the reporting date no service had been performed, no unconditional right to payment existed, no customer cash had arrived, and no associated inventory or expense had been released. Under the supplied contract and recognition rule, this service earns revenue only after performance and acceptance. The entry must therefore be reversed. Whether its origin was a spreadsheet error or deliberate acceleration remains unknown.

The correcting entries reduce revenue and receivables by 40. Current tax expense and tax payable fall by 40×20% = 8. Net income and closing equity fall by 32. No bank transaction occurs.

Every affected total after the service cut-off correction, kCU
ItemDraftCorrected
Revenue / EBITDA / EBIT1,000 / 200 / 160960 / 160 / 120
Pretax profit / current tax / net income140 / 28 / 112100 / 20 / 80
Closing receivables / tax payable200 / 12160 / 4
Closing equity362330
Total assets724684
Liabilities plus equity362 + 362354 + 330
CFO / closing cash64 / 5464 / 54

Now Δreceivables is 40 and Δtax payable is 4. The corrected bridge is 80 + 40 − 40 − 50 + 30 + 4 = 64. Relative to the draft, net income falls 32, the receivable adjustment improves CFO by 40, and the tax-payable adjustment reduces it by 8: −32 + 40 − 8 = 0. Customer receipts remain 960 − (160 − 120) = 920. Reducing cash by the profit correction would invent a payment.

The fictional loan covenant

Atlas's supplied agreement measures only this entity at the year-end test date. Debt is the closing principal; eligible cash is closing cash minus any restricted cash. Net debt is max(0, debt − eligible cash). Covenant EBITDA equals corrected EBIT plus depreciation plus the smaller of actual qualifying severance and a 10 cap. There are no other add-backs, no netting cap on eligible cash, and no acquisition, projection or management-normalization adjustment. Compliance requires positive covenant EBITDA, net debt/covenant EBITDA ≤ 1.0, and eligible cash ≥ 40. All 54 cash is eligible in the base case. These are fictional terms, not a claim about a typical lender.

On the uncorrected draft, covenant EBITDA would be 200 + 10 = 210. Net debt is 230 − 54 = 176; the draft ratio 176/210 = 88/105 is below one. After correction, covenant EBITDA is 160 + 10 = 170, and the ratio is 176/170 = 88/85, about 1.035. The cash test passes with headroom 54 − 40 = 14, but the leverage test fails.

Debt headroom H = maximum ratio × covenant EBITDA − net debt.
Here H = 1×170 − 176 = −6 kCU.
For EBITDA > 0, leverage passes exactly when H ≥ 0; both financial tests must pass.

A shortfall of 6 is a numerator-equivalent gap under these definitions, not a universal instruction to repay 6. Suppose, as an alternative transaction completed by the test time, Atlas pays down 6 from its existing eligible cash. Debt becomes 224 and cash 48: net debt remains 176, so leverage still fails. In the positive-net-debt region, (D − a) − (C − a) = D − C. Eligible cash headroom also shrinks.

An alternative receipt of 6 of new unrestricted equity before measurement raises cash to 60 with debt 230; net debt becomes 170, and both tests pass at the leverage boundary. If that new 6 is immediately used to repay principal, cash is again 54 and debt 224; net debt is still 170. New debt followed by holding the proceeds would raise debt and cash equally, leaving net debt unchanged while potentially changing other terms. These are comparative scenarios, not evidence that any funding was actually received.

A transaction after a past test date does not retroactively change that test. Cure rights, waivers, acceleration, cross-default, classification and notice duties depend on the actual agreement, dates and applicable rules. Do not infer automatic insolvency from this failed ratio, or presume an undocumented waiver. Report the measured breach and request the relevant agreement and authorized interpretation. A denominator at or below zero fails the stated contract; dividing by a negative EBITDA and reporting an apparently low ratio would be meaningless here.

4. Normalize symmetrically and reconnect to business economics

Normalization is an explicitly labeled scenario about recurring economic performance. It changes an analytical comparison, not bank history or the accounting record. An adjustment requires an explanation of why the event will not recur, how the proposed amount was measured, and which other periods and gains receive the same treatment. If evidence is mixed, show a range. Do not relabel a normal cost merely because management chooses when to incur it.

The U.S. SEC staff's Non-GAAP Financial Measures interpretations, Section 100, address recurring cash costs, consistency across periods, unequal treatment of charges and gains, altered recognition and clear labels. The page records a 13 December 2022 update. Those scoped observations motivate our reconciliation discipline; they do not certify Atlas's hypothetical presentation or summarize all disclosure requirements.

Worked example 3: four earnings measures and a profitable growth plan that consumes cash

Management proposes “adjusted EBITDA” of 245: draft EBITDA 200 plus severance 20 plus marketing 25. But the 40 service correction must first be made. Marketing is a recurring activity required to acquire the supplied customers. Suppose evidence supports treating the severance event and the favorable settlement recovery as nonrecurring for a particular forecast. A symmetric calculation is:

Corrected accounting EBITDA 160 + severance 20 − favorable settlement 15 = illustrative normalized EBITDA 165.

The difference from management's 245 is 40 for the accounting correction, 25 for the unjustified marketing exclusion, and 15 for the omitted unfavorable normalization of the gain. Adding back an expense and removing a favorable gain have opposite signs. If expected recurring severance were 5, only 15 would be added back and this forecast's EBITDA would be 160. None of those calculations cancels the actual severance cash payment.

Keep the purpose of each number visible, kCU
MeasureAmountPurpose and boundary
Uncorrected draft EBITDA200Contains the demonstrated 40 revenue error
Corrected accounting EBITDA160Includes actual severance and settlement
Illustrative normalized EBITDA165Assumes both special items are nonrecurring; retains marketing
Contract-defined EBITDA170Applies only the agreement's capped severance add-back

The verified 960 revenue can be represented by 80 completed installations averaging 12 each. In the supplied operating model, variable cost of sales is 7.5 per installation; recurring operating cash commitments are 195, including marketing 25. At unchanged price, quality, costs and mix, within a stated 0–100 installation capacity range, unit contribution is 12 − 7.5 = 4.5. The recurring EBITDA model is 4.5q − 195. Its continuous operating cash-cost break-even is 195/4.5 = 130/3 installations; whole units require at least 44, subject to real demand. At 80 installations it gives 360 − 195 = 165, reconciling the normalization.

That operating break-even excludes interest, taxes, replacement investment and working-capital funding. Depreciation is not a current payment, but productive assets still wear out. Suppose a separate steady-state planning scenario keeps normalized EBITDA 165, depreciation 40 and interest 20, pays the modeled tax of (165 − 40 − 20)×20% = 21, and requires maintenance capital spending 40 with no working-capital change. Cash remaining before principal or distributions is 165 − 20 − 21 − 40 = 84. The maintenance estimate is an explicit planning input, not something proved by depreciation. This 84 is not the actual year's CFO of 64 or actual CFO-minus-capex of 4.

Incremental growth, relative to a clearly specified comparator

Now compare a next-period plan with 20 additional installations against an otherwise identical plan without them. The extra revenue is 20×12 = 240, variable cost 20×7.5 = 150, and no extra recurring operating cash overhead or interest is needed. The incremental equipment outlay is 30 and its period depreciation is 6. New receivables are 48, new inventory 30 and new supplier payables 18. All incremental tax is paid within the period. Demand and usable capacity are supplied conditions; they need commercial evidence in practice.

Incremental EBITDA is 90, EBIT and pretax profit are 84, tax is 16.8, and net income is 67.2. Additional operating working capital is 48 + 30 − 18 = 60. Therefore incremental CFO is 67.2 + 6 − 60 = 13.2, and cash after the 30 investment is −16.8. Directly, incremental collections are 240 − 48 = 192; supplier payments are 150 + 30 − 18 = 162; CFO is 192 − 162 − 16.8 = 13.2.

The incremental balance sheet closes too: Δcash −16.8 + Δreceivables 48 + Δinventory 30 + Δnet PPE (30 − 6) = 85.2. On the other side, new payables 18 + retained incremental income 67.2 = 85.2. Keeping the comparator's closing cash unchanged requires 16.8 of additional funding or other changes. This is a relative funding need, not a complete next-year forecast or proof that interim bills can be paid. The payment calendar may require more cash before customers settle.

Positive unit contribution and accounting profit can accompany cash absorption from investment and growth. That is a coherent benign explanation for a gap, not a guarantee that growth creates value: future margins, maintenance, defaults, financing costs, timing and the opportunity cost of capital remain to be evaluated in corporate finance. Conversely, cutting useful marketing or maintenance can briefly raise cash while weakening the business that must repay lenders.

5. Turn unresolved claims into an evidence plan

A useful request specifies the assertion, exact population and time window, the evidence's origin, and what would change the conclusion. The PCAOB's AS 1105, paragraphs .02 and .05–.10, distinguishes relevant, reliable evidence from mere quantity and includes information that contradicts management's assertions. Independent origin, direct access and reliable controls matter; none makes a document infallible. We borrow that logic for analysis without claiming to have completed an audit.

A prioritized investigation of Atlas
Priority and assertionEvidence to seekDecision it informs
1. Year-end service revenue was earnedComplete relevant ledger entries, contracts, service logs and customer acceptance, including side terms and events immediately before/after the cut-offDetermine which entries require reversal; inspect entry creation/approval separately before making an intent claim
2. The reported cash is available and loan definitions are completeBank balances and restrictions, lender agreement/amendments, test dates and any documented waiver/cure termsCalculate eligibility, all test conditions and immediate funding/action deadlines
3. Remaining receivables and inventory have economic supportInvoice-level aging and matched later receipts/credits; inventory counts, aging, orders and realized selling pricesDistinguish timing from impairment or unsupported balances; consider further corrections
4. Capitalized and normalized amounts reflect their stated natureAsset invoices and service descriptions, evidence of future benefit, depreciation start dates, multi-year severance and settlement recordsCorrect classification or measurement; build symmetric recurring-performance scenarios
5. Growth earns and funds the forecast marginSigned orders, capacity plan, complete cost-to-serve records and dated cash receipts/payments under a downside collection caseEvaluate operational feasibility, margins and financing, not merely the earnings target

Preserve original records and a clear list of versions, definitions, proposed entries and unresolved questions. A late journal, a round amount, covenant pressure or a management explanation can guide investigation; none proves intent alone. Conflicting evidence calls for further work and appropriate review within the real organization's governance. Avoid unsupported accusations and avoid dismissing inconvenient evidence because totals balance.

One common second correction illustrates why the entire statement matters. If a payment already counted as capex actually purchased current maintenance with no future benefit, expense it and reduce PPE. Under our no-current-depreciation-on-that-item convention, pretax income falls by the payment, current tax/payable falls by 20%, and net income falls by 80%. Historical total cash does not change. CFO decreases and investing outflow decreases by the same gross amount; recategorizing cash does not create or destroy it. Exercise 7 traces the complete result.

Reproducible work. Download the original inputs and stipulated evidence facts, exact standard-library benchmark and experiment and instructor guide. Keep them together and run python3 v07-c12-analysis.py. The default output is the service-corrected case. Set premature_revenue to zero to reproduce the uncorrected draft, or set capitalized_repair to 15 for the additional repair scenario. Amounts are exact rational strings in JSON, with no installation, network or output file required. The supplied facts establish the case's corrections; the program cannot authenticate those facts or decide whether a real error is intentional.

Exercises

All amounts are kCU. Use the case's 20% current-tax convention where invoked, with no deferred tax. Unchanged tax cash remains unchanged after a noncash correction. Explain signs, affected accounts and the limits of each inference.

  1. A separate firm has net income 90 and depreciation 20. Operating receivables rise 30, inventory rises 10, trade payables fall 5 and current tax payable rises 4. There are no other noncash items or working-capital movements. Compute CFO and the profit-minus-CFO gap. Capital spending is 40, principal paid 12 and dividends 3; opening cash is 50. Reconcile closing cash. State why the calculation alone does not identify a fictitious sale, and why an acquisition-related receivable increase could not simply be inserted into this bridge.
  2. Start from Atlas's service-corrected statements. Evidence now supports an additional 10 impairment allowance against the remaining receivables. Assume it is a current tax deduction under the supplied rule, involves no write-off or cash receipt/payment, and all other items are unchanged. Find net income, net receivables, tax payable, equity, total assets and CFO. Show the indirect bridge using net receivables. If instead you use gross receivables and add the noncash impairment back, show how to avoid counting it twice. Does the allowance itself establish that the original service never occurred?
  3. Use service-corrected Atlas with covenant EBITDA 170, debt 230 and cash 54. Of that cash, 10 is now known to be restricted and ineligible. Compute net debt, both covenant headrooms and the minimum new unrestricted equity that would satisfy both tests if received before measurement. Compare paying down 8 from existing eligible cash, and borrowing 8 while retaining its proceeds. Assume no fees or earnings changes. Explain the difference between these hypothetical before-test actions and a receipt after an already failed test.
  4. A different company's corrected EBITDA is 130. It includes a cash restructuring charge of 18, a cash litigation recovery of 8 and ordinary recurring launch marketing of 12. Evidence suggests restructuring will recur at 6 each year. Management adds back all 18 and all 12 but retains the gain. Calculate management's measure and a symmetric recurring scenario. Explain the 26 difference, whether historical cash changes, and why a lender's different definition must be calculated separately.
  5. The corrected year-end receivable cohort of 160 comprises 120 not yet due and 40 overdue more than 90 days. Within 45 days after year-end, verified bank receipts settle 100 of the first group and 10 of the overdue group; no other balances or receipts belong to this cohort. Calculate the total settlement percentage and each group's remaining balance. Identify one inference supported by those receipts and two assertions they do not settle. Give a benign and an adverse explanation for the remaining overdue 30 and a concrete next evidence request.
  6. In the incremental growth case of Worked example 3, change only new receivables from 48 to 72 because customers pay more slowly. Keep tax paid equal to the unchanged incremental tax expense. Calculate incremental working capital, CFO, cash after investment and the funding needed to keep the comparator's closing cash unchanged. Reconcile the incremental balance sheet. Does the change in collection timing reduce this period's stipulated profit, and does unchanged profit establish that the plan is fundable on every date?
  7. Start again from the service-corrected Atlas, without the impairment in Exercise 2. Of the recorded 60 capital payment, 15 bought current repair service with no future benefit. No current depreciation was recorded on that item; all reported depreciation 40 relates to valid assets. The cash payment already occurred. Under the supplied rules, correct the repair classification and calculate EBIT, current tax, net income, tax payable, PPE, equity, CFO, investing cash, total cash and both sides of the closing balance sheet. Recalculate covenant EBITDA and debt headroom. Explain why simply subtracting 15 from cash as well would be wrong.
  8. Write a 250-word decision memo for the supplied service-corrected Atlas. Separate established accounting facts, current covenant consequences, a defensible economic scenario and unresolved evidence. Include two competing explanations for the original revenue error; three prioritized evidence requests tied to assertions; and one proposed action whose result depends on a stated condition. Address the claim, “Positive profit and a balancing balance sheet prove the company is safe.” Do not declare fraud or loan acceleration from facts that do not establish them.
Complete solutions and reasoning criteria
  1. CFO is 90 + 20 − 30 − 10 − 5 + 4 = 69; profit minus CFO is 21. Payables fell, so the firm paid more than the associated purchases and the cash adjustment is negative. Cash closes at 50 + 69 − 40 − 12 − 3 = 64. A cash gap can reflect genuine sales timing, inventory and liability movements; there is no transaction evidence here identifying a false sale. Receivables acquired with a business do not represent this entity's current-period uncollected revenue. Their acquisition movement must be separated from the operating movement, with the purchase cash treated under its own classification.
  2. Current tax falls 2 and net income falls 8, giving 72. Net receivables become 150, tax payable 2, equity 322, assets 674, and liabilities plus equity 120 + 2 + 230 + 322 = 674. With net receivables, the bridge is 72 + 40 − (150 − 120) − 50 + 30 + 2 = 64. With gross receivables still 160 and a separate allowance, it is 72 + 40 + 10 − (160 − 120) − 50 + 30 + 2 = 64. Add back the 10 only with the gross receivable movement; adding it to the net-balance version would overstate CFO by 10. The allowance concerns recoverability under the supplied evidence; it does not by itself disprove occurrence of the sale or establish intent.
  3. Eligible cash is 44; net debt is 230 − 44 = 186. Debt headroom is 170 − 186 = −16, and cash headroom is 44 − 40 = 4. New unrestricted equity of 16 raises eligible cash to 60 and reduces net debt to 170, satisfying both gates. Repayment of 8 from existing eligible cash produces debt222, total cash46, eligible cash36 and net debt186: leverage is unchanged and the minimum-cash test now also fails by4. Borrowing8 produces debt238, total cash62, eligible cash52 and net debt186; liquidity headroom rises to12 but leverage still fails. These results assume completed actions before the relevant test. A later receipt does not alter historical balances or establish a contractual cure or waiver.
  4. Management's figure is 130 + 18 + 12 = 160. If recurring restructuring is6, the supported add-back is only18 − 6 =12. Remove the favorable recovery8 and retain recurring marketing12: the scenario is 130 + 12 − 8 = 134. The 26 excess comprises an extra restructuring exclusion6, marketing exclusion12 and retained gain8. Historical payments and receipts do not change. These are explicitly labeled analytical figures based on recurrence assumptions; a covenant may prescribe different permitted items and caps and must be computed from its actual terms.
  5. Matched receipts are 100 + 10 = 110, so the cohort settlement rate is 110/160 = 68.75%. The first group has20 remaining and the overdue group has30, totaling50. The matched bank receipts support actual settlement of those particular balances; they do not establish year-end performance/acceptance or recoverability of the uncollected50. The overdue30 could reflect a documented payment dispute or administrative delay on genuine work; alternatively, it could reflect customer distress, an unsupported charge or an unrecorded concession. Seek customer-specific correspondence, original acceptance/payment terms, credit notes and independently matched subsequent payments. No single aggregate percentage establishes which explanation is true or the correct allowance amount.
  6. Incremental net working capital is 72 + 30 − 18 = 84. Net income remains67.2, because the stipulated revenue and expense recognition facts and tax do not change. CFO is 67.2 + 6 − 84 = −10.8; cash after investment is −10.8 − 30 = −40.8. Keeping comparator cash unchanged requires 40.8 of additional funding or an equivalent change. Δassets = −40.8 + 72 + 30 + 24 = 85.2, equal to Δpayables18 + Δequity67.2. A 24 delay in collections reduces cash by24 relative to the original −16.8 but leaves this supplied profit unchanged. Credit losses or changed contract terms could change profit in a richer case. The annual bridge does not establish interim funding.
  7. Current repair expense reduces EBITDA160 to 145 and EBIT120 to 105. Pretax profit is85, tax 17, net income 68, tax payable17 − 16 = 1. PPE is320 − 15 = 305, and equity330 − 12 = 318. CFO is68 + 40 − 40 − 50 + 30 + 1 = 49. Valid capital spending is45, so investing cash is −45; financing stays−30 and cash is80 + 49 − 45 − 30 = 54. Assets are54 + 160 + 150 + 305 = 669; liabilities plus equity are120 + 1 + 230 + 318 = 669. Covenant EBITDA is145 + 10 = 155; net debt remains176, so debt headroom is −21. The repair payment was already included in historical cash. CFO falls15 and investing cash rises15; subtracting another15 from closing cash would double-count the payment.
  8. Evaluation criteria: a successful memo must use corrected revenue960, net income80, CFO64 and cash54; identify the specified leverage breach while acknowledging the passing cash gate; distinguish the illustrative normalized EBITDA165 from contractual170; include competing unintentional and intentional explanations without asserting either as fact; and connect three requests to decisions. An illustrative memo explains that the service record establishes the40 accounting reversal but not intent; a mapping/cut-off failure and deliberate acceleration remain alternatives. Priority requests are the full contract and acceptance trail, bank restrictions and executed loan terms, and receivable aging/subsequent collection evidence. An unrestricted equity receipt6 would satisfy the numerical tests if actually completed before measurement; a later injection requires the agreement's cure process. Profitable growth can absorb cash, but collections, capacity, maintenance and financing still need support. A balanced statement is necessary arithmetic discipline and can contain unsupported entries. Award credit for other evidence-supported priorities; do not award it for inventing a waiver, alleging fraud from a ratio, replacing covenant definitions with preferred adjustments, or asserting solvency from one annual snapshot.

Teach-back and delayed check

Teach-back task. In five minutes, explain why correcting 40 of unearned revenue reduces net income by32 but leaves cash unchanged, why the correction creates a covenant breach, and why paying down debt with existing cash does not necessarily repair it. End with one benign and one adverse hypothesis for weak cash conversion and the evidence that distinguishes them.

Teach-back benchmark

Reverse revenue/receivable40 and current tax/payable8. Equity and profit fall32; the indirect cash effects −32 + 40 − 8 cancel because no money moved. Net debt stays176 while covenant EBITDA falls210 to170, crossing the ratio limit. Existing-cash repayment reduces debt and eligible cash equally; new unrestricted equity changes net debt. Genuine growth with slow customer payment can absorb cash; unsupported revenue or deteriorating recoverability can also produce a gap. Match service acceptance and customer terms to the cut-off, and match invoice-level later receipts and credits to aging. A red flag identifies work to do, not the answer about intent.

Delayed check, 7–14 days later. Use the original draft, but suppose the established service reversal is30 rather than40, and10 of the closing cash is restricted. No repair correction applies. Find corrected net income, receivables, tax payable, CFO, covenant EBITDA and both headrooms. Find the minimum new unrestricted equity that would satisfy both gates if actually received before measurement. Then explain how collecting20 of valid existing receivables, with no fee or earnings change, affects net debt and profit.

Delayed-check answer

Pretax profit is140 − 30 =110; tax22; net income88. Receivables170, tax payable6 and equity338 reconcile assets694 with liabilities356 + equity338. CFO is88 + 40 − 50 − 50 + 30 + 6 = 64; cash remains54. Covenant EBITDA is200 − 30 + 10 = 180; eligible cash44 means net debt186. Debt headroom is−6, cash headroom4. New unrestricted equity6 yields eligible cash50 and net debt180, passing both gates. As a separate alternative, collecting20 of valid receivables raises cash74, leaves restricted cash10, and reduces eligible-net debt to230 − 64 = 166; receivables fall150. It changes neither revenue nor profit, and is a current cash event rather than the earlier noncash correction. All test results remain tied to the actual measurement date.

Volume synthesis and extension. Recognition determines what enters the accounts; estimates and policy determine measurement; cash and financing determine payment capacity; operating economics determines what can persist. Carry the reconciled statements and explicit hypotheses into the volume assessment and corporate finance and valuation. Deeper investigations require transaction-level evidence, applicable standards and agreements, appropriate specialists and an actual engagement scope. This chapter supplies a reproducible analytical method and a disciplined account of what remains unknown.

Sources and further study

  • PCAOB — AS 2401: Consideration of Fraud in a Financial Statement Audit — Distinguish intentional misstatement from error; suspicious conditions can have other explanations; limits of inference and audit assurance.
  • PCAOB — AS 1105: Audit Evidence — Evidence relevance, reliability, source, precision and contradictory information; tie each request to an assertion.
  • SEC Division of Corporation Finance — Non-GAAP Financial Measures interpretations, Section 100, updated 13 December 2022 — Recurring operating costs, consistent and symmetric adjustments, recognition principles and clear measure labels.
  • IFRS Foundation — IAS 7 Statement of Cash Flows: public About overview — Direct and indirect cash-flow logic, activity classification and noncash exclusions; source scope separate from the fictional case conventions.
